Executive Summary 
With the goal of improving financial resilienc e and risk -informed investment planning, the 
European Union, in collaboration with the World Bank and the GFDRR, has started a program 
for “Strengthening Financial Resilience and Accelerating Risk Reduction in Central Asia” (SFRARR), aiming 
to advance disaster and climate resilience in Central Asia countries, which includes Kazakhstan, 
Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. The program includes several 
operational components, all contributing to the development of a comprehensive probabilistic risk 
assessment, consistent across multiple hazards and asset types of the target countries. 
Central Asia is an area characterized by complex tectonic and active deformation. The related 
seismic activity controls the earthquake hazard lev el that, due to the occurrence of secondary and 
tertiary effects, has also direct implications on the hazard related to mass movements (e.g., 
landslides and naturally dammed lake outbursts). Note that in Central Asia landslides, mudslides 
and debris flows are causing an extensive number of casualties every year. Climatically, this region 
is characterized by strong rainfall gradient contrasts, due to the diversity of climate and vegetation 
zones. The region is drained by large, partly snow - and glacier-fed mountain rivers, that cross or 
terminate in arid forelands. Central Asian countries are therefore affected by a significant river 
flood hazard, mainly in spring and summer seasons. The challenge posed by this combination of 
different hazards can only be tackled considering a multi-hazard approach harmonized among the 
different countries, in agreement with the requirements of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk 
Reduction, approved at the third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in 2015. 
This re port describes the methodology and results  of Task 3, Fluvial and Pluvial Flood Hazard 
Assessment, within the “Regionally consistent risk assessment for earthquakes and floods and 
selective landslide scenario analysis for strengthening financial resilience and accelerating 
risk reduction in Central Asia” project. Flood hazard assessment was carried out by means of a 
physically based  numerical modelling toolset and a stochastic catalogue of flood footprints . In 
particular, the report includes the following topics: 
• In Section 1, a brief introduction, describing the scope of Task 3, state of the art of flood 
hazard assessment and summary of our methodology. 
• Section 2 describes the available global and local datasets 
• The following Sections are dedicated to the presentation and validation of the modeling 
toolset, which include the  hydrological model TOPKAPI (Section  3), Extreme Value 
Analysis (Section 4) and the hydraulic model CA2D (Section 5) 
• In Section 6 we present three realistic flood scenarios that have not happened in the past 
but may affect the region in the future. 
• The generation of the stochastic catalogue is described in Section 7 
• Section 8 focuses on the climate change scenario 
• Section 9 is dedicated to pluvial flood modeling  
• Finally, in Section 10 we present our work’s strengths and limitations as well as 
recommendations for future users 
• Annexes 1, 2, 3 and 4 contain all flood hazard maps (fluvial undefended, fluvial defended, 
fluvial future scenario, pluvial)

1 Introduction 
 Scope of Task 3 – Flood hazard assessment 
Central Asia is highly exposed and vulnerable to a broad range of natural hazards which frequently 
result in economic and human losses. Flood hazard is significant in the region, with floods being 
the most frequent natural disaster in the period 1988-2007 according to a recent analysis provided 
by the Central Asia and Caucasus Disaster Risk Management Initiative (CAC DRMI, 2009). In the 
same period, floods were second for number of deaths and amount of population affected (1,512 
and 19% respectively). Despite the aridity of large areas in some of the target countries, natural 
phenomena linked to extreme precipitation can cause billions of dolla rs of damages every year : 
collectively, floods inflict the second highest overall economic losses ($52 million), surpassed only 
by earthquake (an annual average of $186 million). At the local level  (e.g., in Tajikistan), flood is 
sometimes the dominant risk in terms of economic losses  (World Bank et al., 2012). Considering 
the deteriorated protection infrastructure and vulnerabilities in several sectors, floods cause 
considerable damage to housing, infrastructure, and agriculture (Libert, 2008). 
A robust estimation of poss ible loss due to flood is necessary for developing and implementing 
successful regional DRM strategies as advocated for by the past World Conferences for Disaster 
Risk Reduction (UNDRR, 2019). In order to support the development of regional DRFI solutions, 
and to inform DRM/DRR activities in the region, in this study we assess fluvial and pluvial flood 
hazard to be used as input to characterize flood risk in Central Asia. We adopted a hybrid stochastic 
and physically based approach, which takes into account the scale of the phenomenon, the data 
available (both input data and calibration/validation data) and potential future modification to the 
hazard triggered by climate change. 
For the purpose of this study, we distinguish two common types of floods: fluvial flood , which 
occurs when excessive rainfall over an extended period of time causes a river to exceed its capacity, 
and pluvial flood, which occurs  when heavy rainfall creates a flood event unrelated to  an 
overflowing water body. The final deliverables are: 
a) Fluvial and pluvial flood hazard maps for current climate over the entire Central Asia area 
including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic , Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan for 
selected return periods (5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 years) ; fluvial flood hazard for 
current climate is assessed in both undefended and defended scenarios and a variability 
range is also provided for the undefended case 
b) A hazard-consistent stochastic catalogue of fluvial flood footprints, which is essential for 
characterizing risk and supporting DRM strategies 
c) Fluvial flood hazard maps for the same selected return periods obtained taking into account 
the impact of climate change for a 2080 scenario . Fluvial flood hazard for current climate 
is assessed in both undefen ded and defended scenarios and a variability range is also 
provided for the undefended case 
d) Hazard curves at five selected locations 
e) Flood footprint for one historical scenario used to validate the CA2D hydraulic model 
f) Flood footprint for three realistic s cenarios across the region representing potential flood 
events with 100-year return period that may occur in populated and flood-prone areas.

The proposed modelling approach, which leverages on the use of reanalysis data available in near 
real time  (e.g., ERA5-Land) and o n a hydrological/hydraulic modelling chain calibrated using 
historical observed data, is potentially suitable for the implementation of Disaster Risk Financing 
applications based on parametric triggers  (e.g., CCRIF for the Caribbean and Cen tral America 
regions, ARC for the continent of Africa).  
The development of a regional model cannot be done without the contribution of experts from 
the local scientific community. Partnership with local governmental institutions and authorities is 
also an essential step to facilitate model acceptance and for potential integration with national 
models. Following this concept, the consortium has engaged with the local communities for 
building and extending awareness of flood hazard and for enhancing the technical capacity of local 
experts in the use of open tools and resources (see Table 1 for the complete list of involved

 Previous regional and global hazard studies 
Regional flood hazard assessment for Central Asia is usually included in more comprehensive risk 
studies. A study on flood hazard of the territories in the Esil Water Management Basin  in 
Kazakhstan was conducted in 2019 (Plekhanov and Medeu, 2019). In Kyrgyz Republic, a catalogue 
of historical floods and hazard maps is managed by the Ministry of Emergency Situations of the 
Kyrgyz Republic (MES). At the global scale, there are various flood hazard assessment models that 
provide hazard maps at various resolutions and considering different return periods. Some 
examples are the Catchment-Based Macro-scale Floodplain (CaMa-Flood) model (Yamazaki et al., 
2011), the Centro Internazionale in Monitoraggio Ambientale and United  Nations Environment 
Program (CIMA-UNEP) model  (Rudari et al., 2015) , the European Centre for  Medium-Range 
Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) model (Pappenberger et al., 2012), the Global Flood Risk with Image 
Scenarios (GLOFRIS) model  (Ward et al., 2013)  which is implemented in the Aqueduct Floods 
platform (Ward, P. J. et al., 2020) , the Joint Research Cent re (JRC) model  (Dottori et al., 2016)  
based on the Copernicus Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS) (Alfieri et al., 2013), and the 
Fathom Global  Ltd model (Sampson et al., 2015) . For these models, the corresponding flood

 Methodology overview 
In this study, the flood hazard of five Central Asian countries (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic , 
Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan) is assessed by means of a physically based numerical 
modelling toolset and a stochastic catalogue of flood footprints  (Figure 1). The numerical 
modelling toolset is composed of two elements: the hydrological model (TOPKAPI) and the 
hydraulic model (CA2D). A statistical correction of extreme values and their regionaliza tion are 
also performed based on the availability of a historical records of daily and annual maxima 
discharges.  
 
Figure 1. Fluvial flood hazard assessment: schematic representation of methodology 
The TOPKAPI (TOPographic Ki nematic APproximation and Integration) model is a fully -
distributed physically-based hydrological model that can provide high resolution information on 
the hydrological state of a catchment (Ciarapica and Todini, 2002). The TOPKAPI model requires 
as input both precipitation and temperature meteorological data, plus a description of the soil 
characteristics that can be derived from the land use (to derive crop factors and surface roughness) 
and soil type maps (to derive soil permeability and depth).  
CA2D (Dottori and Todini, 2011)  is a full physically -based hydraulic model specifically designed 
for high-performance computing applications, based on the cellular automata (CA) approach and 
the diffusive wave equations, to simulate flood inundation events involving wide areas. The model

is based on the state -of-the-art of large-scale hydraulic modelling and has been tested extensively 
on several case studies.  The CA2D model has an internal preprocessor that allow the user to 
provide as input only the Digital E levation Model and the surface roughness map. The network 
(comprising nodes and links) is automatically generated, and specific conditions (such as flood 
protections) can be included where present. In addition, input meteorological data must be 
provided in the form of hydrographs at specific points and/or of rainfall maps.  
The two models are linked together as shown in Figure 1: (1) the TOPKAPI  hydrological 
simulation results informs the (2) Extreme Value Analysis and regionalization, which produces a 
stochastic description of streamflow from which peak flows values are extracted (1-in-5, 10, 20, 50, 
100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000 years floods) and used as input for the (3) CA2D hydraulic model, which 
simulates the channels routing as well as the 2D inundation processes to derive the (4) hazard maps. 
Finally, the hazard-consistent stochastic catalogue of flood footprints for the region is produced.  
While hazard maps provide the probability and depth of inundation at a given location, they are 
unable to describe the likelihood of concurrent floo ding across multiple sites, limiting their 
capability of assessing risk over the full range of plausible scenarios, including the most extreme 
ones which are the very thing insurers must quantify for pricing and liquidity. A flood hazard 
catalogue serves this purpose, by providing a stochastic ensemble of 10,000 years of all hypothetical 
floods, with related annual frequency of occurrence, that may occur in the region of interest. To 
ensure spatial coherence in the stochastic catalogue, the spatial correlation of the river flow at each 
gauge/station is determined by computing a cross correlation matrix on all the available 
(observed/simulated) flow time series. The procedure is detailed in Section 7. 
 
The Extreme Value Analysis and regionalization process consists of two steps: a) a correction of 
the TOPKAPI simulated discharge based on the historical record of observed data, which allows 
for better representing the extreme values simulated during the period 1981 -2020, and b) the 
estimation of General Extreme Value distribution for several locations along the drainage network 
to derive the peak flows with different return periods.  Additional details will be given in Sections 
3 to 8. 
Pluvial flood hazard is estimated a pplying a similar methodology (Figure 2), where, to reduce the 
computational effort, a geomorphological technique is combined to the CA2D hydraulic 
simulations. First, annual maxima precipitation for different durations derived from ERA5 -Land 
gridded data, which are available from 1981 to present, are corrected based on their comparison 
with the station data from the KNMI Climate Explorer dataset. This correction was nec essary to 
take into account the unavoidable discrepancy between point data and gridded data. In fact, the 
latter represent the average precipitation over an area of about 100 km2 and does not well describe 
the extremes that may occur in smaller sectors. Th e corrected ERA5 -Land annual maxima 
precipitation is eventually used to derive Intensity -Duration-Frequency curves, from which the 
precipitation at different return periods is extracted to feed the CA2D hydraulic model. The CA2D 
model is applied to several areas and the output are used to calibrate the geomorphological 
technique based on the Compound Topographic Index to extend the si mulation to the entire 
region. Additional details will be given in Section 9. 
We did not include the generation of a pluvial flood hazard stochastic catalogue becaus e pluvial 
flood is a much more local phenomena and, on such a large area, it requires an impractical

2 Data Collection 
Both the hydrological and the hydraulic model require daily or sub-daily hydrometeorological data 
as well as spatially distributed information such as soil characteristics, land use , elevation, and the 
presence of hydraulic structures and reservoirs . With the aim of obtaining a homogeneous and 
regionally consistent  hazard assessment, we integrated the ground local data , available from 
historical observations and previous national and regional studies, with spatially distributed global 
datasets. 
Specifically, t he TOPKAPI hydrological model requires daily or sub -daily precipitation and 
temperature records as input data  and d ischarge time series at daily/sub daily resolution for 
calibration and validation. Discharge time series are also used to characterize the statistical behavior 
of extreme flows through the analysis of annual maxima , which is essential to produce the inputs 
for CA2D hydraulic simulations. CA2D also requires a detailed digital elevation model to define 
the boundary conditions of the domai n. Both TOPKAPI and CA2D require spatially distributed 
information for the characterization of the river catchments  and flow behavior (infiltration and 
roughness). Data on defensive protections and the presence of regulated/unregulated reservoirs 
and dams is also critical for accurately assess flood hazard, as a misrepresentation of these structures 
can lead to over/underestimation of flow and water depth magnitude and frequency. Unfortunately, 
information regarding hydraulic defenses is rare and very difficult to obtain because a 
comprehensive database is usually not available at country level, and it is considered classified. 
 Local data 
We held multiple individual meetings with our partners located in the targeted countries to illustrate 
our methodology and the data needed to accomplish the flood hazard assessment. We also clarified 
the requested data temporal resolution and format. Specifically, we focused our data requests on: 
1. Historical records of discharge data at daily or sub -daily temporal res olution. Alternatively, 
records of monthly or annual maximum discharge. 
2. Information on fluvial hydraulic protections including the poly -lines of the protections and 
potential information on height and protection level. 
3. Location of lakes and reservoirs potentially including the polygons describing their spatial extent 
and associated with information on volume, operational rules, relation volume-level, relation level-
discharge. 
There was a large variability in  the type and quality of the data p rovided. Specifically, for most 
countries, obtaining daily discharge data was a long process that required several external meetings 
and official requests to the partner Countries’ Ministries. Another common issue was digitization, 
as data from local partners were typically on paper form. Finally, all local partners made clear that 
a comprehensive database of hydraulic protection data has never been compiled at country level in 
any of the targeted countries and this type of information is  considered highly classified and 
confidential. Unfortunately, it would be extremely difficult to obtain it even at a low level of detail. 
Hence, all the local institutions that we contacted stressed the impossibility to disseminate such 
confidential information.

3 Hydrological Modeling 
The TOPKAPI (Ciarapica and Todini, 2002) hydrological model is a well-established, cutting-edge 
tool derived upon the assumption that the horizontal flow at a point in the soil and over the surface 
can be approximated by means of a kinematic wave model. The model was first developed around 
20 years ago, and then constantly updated to keep up with the latest advances in the field . The 
consortium holds an internal version of the TOPKAPI model, which was set up at the catchment 
scale in order to optimize its performances in terms of computational times over the entire Central 
Asia region. The model w as run with a hourly time step and 1-km spatial resolution. The model 
was applied to all major catchments in the countries of study, including transboundary catchments, 
also covering areas in China, Afghanistan and Russia that contribute to the runoff of the rivers 
crossing the targeted countries. 
 Model Setup 
TOPKAPI is a fully distributed physically based hydrological model that combines the kinematic 
approach with the topography of  the basin described by means of a lattice of square cell s. Each 
cell represents a computational node for the physical characteristics of the model, namely the mass 
balance and the momentum balance. TOPKAPI takes precipitation and temperature 
meteorological data as inputs and evaluates the flow paths from the DEM. C rop factors, surface 
roughness, soil permeability and depth are derived from land -use and soil -type maps and  are 
utilized to simulate infiltration and flow behavior.  
The TOPKAPI model includes a specific module for managing reservoirs  and regulated lakes . 
However, it needs to be calibrated with specific information on the operation strategies and/or 
volume/level curves  for all reservoirs . Since such data w ere not generally available for the 
simulation domain, we did not include the lake module within the TOPKAPI configuration but 
took eventually into consideration the effect of reservoirs by correcting the resulting flow curves 
in the river branches downstream dams using the procedure explained in Section 4.1.2. 
Figure 10 schematically represents the structure of the TOPKAPI model and highlights the main 
hydrological processes that are simulated: snowmelt, evapotranspiration, three levels of horizontal 
flow (overland, sub-surface and channel), infiltration, and percolation.

 Calibration and Validation Results 
The TOPKAPI model was calibrated through a trial-and-error procedure adapting the initial model 
parameters in order to match the available observed discharge. We mainly based the model 
calibration on the historical daily data, but also used the annual maxima for the areas where daily 
data were not available. Given that the objective of the hydrological simulations  is the derivation 
of the extreme discharge value distribut ions over several river sections across the region to 
eventually feed the hydraulic model to derive the flood footprint at different return periods, the 
calibration process focused on reproducing the flow peaks. Since a physically based model 
reproduces better the flow peaks if all the other hydrological components are well represented, we 
made sure that the main hydrological processes were also correctly reproduced, with particular 
attention to the snow accumulation/melting component, which is the driver of most of the floods 
affecting the region. The calibration has been performed independently for each catchment where 
historical data were available. Given the distributed and physically based nature of the TOPKAPI 
hydrological model, the calibration process was not based on an automatic procedure but on the

precipitation, snow melting, evapotranspiration and river volume) and evaluation

used in the first step of the loop 
This procedure allows the identification of model parameters values that provide reasonable

4 Extreme Value Analysis and Adjustment 
In order to assess fluvial flood hazard, we need to characterize the statistical behavior of extreme 
flows through the analysis of annual maxima. This is done using the simulated discharge data 
produced during the hydrologic simulations together with historical discharge data collected from 
local and global sources (see Table 2 and Table 3). A great wealth of flow data is available to be 
exploited, especially in high -and medium-exposure areas, with some very long historical records  
(see Figure 3 and Figure 4) even dating back to the 1930s-40s-50s. 
The hydrological model was used to obtain a spatially distributed representation of the fluvial flood 
hazard that covers homogeneously all the geographical extension of the target countries. This goal 
was impossible to attain using only observed data. However, the model results have some 
limitations, summarized here, and described in detail in the next paragraphs: 
• Spatial changes in extreme value behaviors: rivers can significantly alter the patterns of 
extreme flows as the flow downward, especially if they are crossing a large alluvial plain, 
with low to almost null slopes and space for inundation. This is often the case in Central 
Asia, where very large alluvial plains crossed by major rivers exist. Hydrological models are 
generally not suited to reproduce accurately the peak flow reduction caused by alluvia l 
plains (see Section 4.1.2). 
• Temporal changes in extreme value behaviors: the construction of large reservoirs typically 
reduces peak flows and alters temporal extreme flow patterns, but accurate data for the 
characterization of reservoirs (depth vs volume curves, spillways and outlet shape, 
operational rules, etc.) are rarely available (see Section 4.1.2). 
• Model uncertainty: despite having been calibrated against observed data, the results of the 
hydrological model are unavoidably affected by errors and biases (as is always the case with 
mathematical models) (see Section 4.1.3). 
To overcome these limitations, historical data can be exploited. H istorical discharge data reveal 
temporal shifts in flow that are observed after a man -made hydraulic structure is built  (e.g., dam, 
regulated reservoir) . Historical discharge data are also useful for accurately represent ing flow 
behavior in Central Asia large floodplains. Observing the spatial shift s in the extreme flow values 
signal, it is possible to represent the natural peak flow reduction consequent to the flood water 
expanding in the floodplains , a phenomenon that  cannot be simulated through hydrological 
modeling. Historical data were also used to identify potential modeling errors and correct them.

Adjustment of simulated flows was based on the comparison of observed and simulated extreme

5 Hydraulic Modeling  and fluvial flood hazard maps 
derivation 
The CA2D hydraulic model was developed and validated  by Dottori and Todini (Dottori and 
Todini, 2011) and uses a 2D Cellular Automata (CA) approach. A Cellular Automata (CA) is a cell-
centered, finite volume scheme for the description of physical dynamic systems regulated  only by 
local laws. In this scheme, each cell assumes a certa in state (or property), which evolves in time 
according to specified fixed rules. In CA2D case, the momentum equation is solved for each time 
step, computing volume exchanges between grid cells along the cell’s borders. Volumes of each 
cell are successively updated using flow volume conservative equations. We ran the model using 
the semi -inertial form ulation of the momentum equation , which was developed for the 
LISFLOOD-FP model (Bates et al., 2010). This approach allows for high resolution simulations at 
a significantly reduced computational effort, making it possible to run hydraulic simulations at the 
continental and global scale (Dottori and Todini, 2011).  
 Model Setup 
The consortium holds an internal version of the CA2D model, which was implemented in C++ 
programming language and fully parallelized via Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) to improve its 
performance in terms of computational time. The model was run with a 0.00083° (~90 m) spatial 
resolution. The simulation time -step is dynamic, and it varies between 0.01 and 15 seconds, with 
the maximum allowable time step defined by  the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy or CFL condition , 
which is commonly adopted to preserve stability in computational fluid dynamics models. 
The stochastic catalogue of streamflow produced via the Extreme Value Analysis (see Section 4) 
was used to derive the simulated flood hydrographs that serve as input to CA2D. The hydraulic 
model also takes spatially distributed data as inputs, such as the DEM and roughness to define the 
computation grid and determine the flow diffusion and velocity.  For this purpose we used the 
MERIT DEM (Karnieli et al., 2010) (Figure 5) together with MERIT Hydro (Yamazaki et al., 2019). 
Land use maps for GlobeLand30 (Figure 7) were used instead to derive roughness values.  
Flow diffusion describes the water volume exchanges between grid cells, by integrating the semi -
inertial momentum equation along the cells’ connections which are called links. The computation 
grid can have various link network configurations, in our application, we adopted a four direction 
link network, which is better suited for large scale studies and Central Asia's geomorphology 
(Dottori, 2012). Then, flow volumes are updated at each time step following the conservative 
equation. The result is a flood footprint of the maximum water depth at each cell over the 
simulation.

 Uncertainty 
The assessment of the model u ncertainty is important for a proper interpretation of the results . 
Uncertainty sources include: 
• input data (precipitation and discharge); 
• hydrological modelling; 
• hydraulic modelling. 
A proper uncertainty assessment is only possible if an adequate number of observations is available. 
In the case of the present modelling approach, observed flow data are available, thus allowing the 
estimation of the uncertainty of the results of the hydrological model. For this reaso n, the 
methodology followed here is based on the analysis of the hydrological model bias at gauged river 
sections. Such an uncertainty estimation includes errors stemming from input precipitation and 
temperature data and conceptual hydrological model appro ximations and simplifications. It does 
not include errors introduced by conceptual simplifications made within the hydraulic model, 
because observed water depth data is not available.  In any case, the errors introduced by the 
hydraulic model are typically much smaller than the ones from the hydrological model. 
The uncertainty analysis was carried out by comparing the modelled discharge extreme values 
distributions after bias correction with the observed ones (both obtained through a GEV fittin g, 
see previous sections for more information). Absolute values of percent errors were computed on 
pairs of observed vs . simulated flows at fixed return periods (5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 
years) for every river section w here observed data were ava ilable. Then, for every return period, 
the empirical 90% percentile of all percent errors in all gauged stations was computed. The 
corresponding values of percent errors were used to obtain lower and upper bounds of discharge 
extreme values distributions at gauged sections.  
For ungauged sections, a similar procedure was put in place, but rather than comparing extreme 
values distributions  from simulations and observations ( obviously not available at ungauged 
sections), the comparison was done on distributions before and after the bias correction. The final 
result was, again, lower and upper bounds of discharge extreme values distributions. 
The resulting upper and lower bound peak discharges were used to obtain upper and lower bound 
hazard maps for every retu rn period through flood simulations with the CA2D model. The 
uncertainty in the fluvial flood simulations is therefore presented through a set of two maps for 
each return period, representing the bilateral 80% confidence interval of the water depth estimation 
in the hazard maps.

7 Stochastic Catalogue 
A stochastic catalogue of events is a set of plausible flood footprints that did not occur in the past 
but that are generated synthetically to be statistically consistent with the historical flood footprints 
in terms of extent, water depth and frequency of occurrence. A stochastic catalogue is necessary to 
obtain a reliable assessment of the losses, especially those caused by rare and very rare floods, with 
return periods much longer than the length of the historical record (40 years in this case).  When 
building a stochastic catalog for risk assessment purpose s the consideration of spatial correlation 
is fundamental, especially to obtain a reliable loss exceedance probability curve that consider the 
probability of having simultaneous events in different areas of the region. To build the stochastic 
catalogue we derived the correlation among the virtual stations based on the TOPKAPI simulated 
annual maximum discharge over the historical period (see Section 3) and aggregated the virtual 
stations into clusters based on their location, correlation, and accumulated are a. Therefore, the 
clusters represent groups of virtual stations with high probability to have a simultaneous flood 
during the same rainfall event, while in virtual stations belonging to different clusters the probability 
to have concurrent floods is low, or even null. 
The methodology followed to produce a stochastic catalogue consists of the following steps: 
1. Clustering: virtual stations are grouped into clusters, under the assumption that flows at 
virtual stations in the same cluster are highly correlated random variables (Figure 38). As 
mentioned above, t his step is based on correlations among historical simulated flows, 
location of the stations and accumulated areas of the stations. 
2. Cluster activation probability : the annual probability of activation of a cluster is computed, 
where “activation” is defined when at least one virtual station in a given cluster exceeds the 
5-year flow. This probability is based on the activation of clusters in the historical simulated 
flows. 
3. Activation of virtual stations within a cluster : the average number of active virtual stations for a 
given year as well as its standard deviation  are computed. An active station is defined as 
such when it exceeds the 5-year flow. These values are based on the activation of cluster s 
in the historical simulated flows. 
4. Generation of the stochastic catalogue: based on all the analysis above (clusters, annual activation 
probability, average number of active stations) and on the hazard curves at each virtual 
station, a stochastic catalogue is produced, with equivalent duration of 10,000 years, where 
every year consists in an annual flood footprint, i.e., a map where each pixel represents the 
maximum water depth during a given year. 
The complete procedure is described in the following paragraphs. 
 
 Clustering 
We first took 40 years of simulated discharge (1981 -2020) and computed the annual maxima for 
each TOPKAPI station.  
Each station was then associated to a cluster based on the annual maximum discharge correlation, 
location and flow accumulated area. In this phase the following assumptions were made:

• Catchments are independent; therefore, a cluster cannot include virtual stations belonging

• Catchments with area smaller than 5,000 km2 become independent clusters. 
The clusters were formed adopting a hierarchical clustering based on a condensed distance matrix 
(Johnson, 1967; Murtagh and Contreras, 2017, 2012) . Hierarchical clustering (also called 
hierarchical cluster analysis or HCA) is an unsupervised technique to partition data into 
homogeneous groups called clusters. In order to decide which elements should be combined, a 
measure of dissimilarity between sets of observation is requi red. Typically, this is achieved by 
defining a distance metric (a measure of distance between pairwise observations) and a linkage 
criterion which defines from which cluster point the distance is calculated. 
We built the distance matrix as a weighted combination of the correlation matrix and the Gower’s 
distance matrix (Gower, 1971)  computed from the station’s location (coordinates) and flow 
accumulated area. As linkage criterion we selected the Ward method which minimizes the total 
within-cluster variance (Ward, 1963).

8 Climate Change scenario 
Central Asia experiences very large temperature fluctuations, which are ex pected to increase in 
severity and frequency due to climate change. The effects of a changing climate are already visible 
today, with noticeably higher temperatures and an increase in extreme weather events frequency 
and severity in recent decades (Hydrometeorological Service under the Cabinet of Ministers of the 
Republic of Uzbekistan, 2009; Ministry of Environment Protection Kazakhstan, 2009; State 
Agency for Hydrometeorology of Tajikistan, 2009; State Agency on Environment Protection and 
Forestry under the Government of the Kyrgyz Republic, 2009) . Over the course of 80 years, all 
countries have seen an increase in annual average temperatures that significantly exceeds global 
trends. The countries of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic , and Tajikistan experienced the highest 
temperature increase in the winter peri od, while in Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan the most 
significant changes were observed in the summer and autumn months. Even if a regional clear 
trend in precipitation was not observed, precipitation variability and the frequency of intense 
rainfall events have consistently increased in all countries, especially in the mountain areas where 
two-thirds of the region’s population is concentrated1. 
Higher temperatures triggered by climate change are expected to significantly affect the 
hydrological cycle in the region, especially for what concerns both the snow accumulation/melting, 
which represents one of the main drivers of fluvial floods in the area, and the evapotranspiration 
processes, which may reduce water availability in the dry periods and increase the wa ter demand 
for irrigation. 
Our goal is to evaluate the change in fluvial flood hazard for a 2080 scenario. The analysis is based 
on climate change scenarios over the region a vailable through the data repositor ies of the 
Copernicus climate data store  (Alos et al. , 2019)  and the Coordinated Regional Climate 
Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX) project database (Giorgi et al., 2009).

9 Pluvial Flood 
The modelling approach described in the previous sections covers fluvial floods, i.e., inundations 
caused by medium to l arge-sized rivers, while localized heavy precipitation bursts might not be 
accurately reproduced. This is a crucial issue for several areas of the region, which are characterized by 
short and intense floods, such as the mountainous areas of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, that may trigger 
catastrophic mudslides as often observed in the past.  
In order to assess pluvial flood hazard in Central Asia, we fed the CA2D model with extreme 
precipitation events based on the Intensity-duration-Frequency (IDF) curves  derived from ground 
stations observations and remotely sensed data. Spatial correlation is taken into account through the 
definition of a cross -correlation matrix estimated on the historical rainfall intensity time series. The 
infiltration rate is also taken i nto account as a function of the land use and soil type classes as well as 
the presence of urban areas. This ensures that the model is calibrated and validated specifically for the 
study area. Excess of rainfall is routed using the model propagation equati ons over selected areas and 
used to calibrate a geomorphological index in order to derive water depths over the entire model 
domain.  
 Data processing 
9.1.1 Derivation of Intensity-Duration-Frequency curves 
The first step to assess pluvial hazard was the derivation of the Intensity-duration-Frequency (IDF) 
curves over the  entire region. The IDF curves represent the distribution of the extreme 
precipitation for different duration s and have been derived according to the ERA5 -Land 
precipitation data for each grid cell and for the durations of 3, 6 and 9 hours, which represent the 
most critical durations for pluvial flood formation. In order to derive the IDF curves, the ERA5 -
Land data were spatially aggregated to tiles of 0.4°x0.4° resolution , and for each tile the annual 
maximum values of precipitation corresponding to the above-mentioned durations were computed 
and fitted with a Gumbel distribution.  
As already mentioned in Section 2.2, precipitation data from ERA5 -Land represent volumes 
averaged over the grid cells, whose size is about 100 km 2. The spatial averaged precipitation 
maintains the average volumes of precipitation in the area and is suitable for hydrological modelling 
purposes and for fluvial flood hazard assessment, but it unavoida bly leads to underestimating the 
local peaks of rainfall that drive the pluvial hazard. For this reason, before deriving the IDF curves, 
a comparison between ERA5-Land and the KNMI Climate Explorer (CE) precipitation data was 
performed to evaluate the magnitude of the gridded data bias with respect to the point station data.

effort 
To reduce the  computational effort required for a fully physically based pluvial flood simulation 
over such a wide region, we took advantage of the geomorphological characteristics of the terrain, 
which is the main driver of potential pluvial floods together with the precipitation intensity and 
duration. In fact, we  first identified a set of relevant areas, evenly distributed across the domain,

to produce the hazard maps over the rest of the region.  The CTI was developed by Beven and 
Kirkby within the runoff model TOPMODEL (Beven and Kirkby, 1979).

10 Concluding Remarks 
  Strengths and limitations 
The results presented herein constitute the first attempt to date at assessing flood hazard in Central 
Asia at a regional scale using a uniform methodology and a homogenized dataset that includes both 
global and local data sources. The cooperation with local partners was productive and gave the 
consortium access to a set of unprecedented local datasets and information as well as technical 
advice. The p artnership with local governmental ins titutions and authorities also offers the  
potential for integration with national models. Therefore, the main strength of this project is the 
combination of state -of-the-art global flood modeling techniques with an unprecedented use of 
local data and knowledge that allowed for a sound hazard assessment over such a wide area. 
The proposed modelling approach  is also potentially suitable for the implementation of Disaster 
Risk Financing applications based on parametric triggers  (e.g., CCRIF for the Caribbean a nd 
Central America regions, ARC for the continent of Africa).  
The main limitation remains the general lack of water depth observations for validating the 
hydraulic model output as well as specific data on hydraulic defense structures, their location, level 
of protection and maintenance. We understand the impossibility of sharing sensible information 
and believe we made the most accurate assumptions given the available data. However, we 
recognize that the presence of dikes can have a non-negligible localized effect on flood hazard. 
As for pluvial hazard, we included the effect of urban drainage but we had to assume the urban 
and non-urban infiltration rates (5% and 30% respectively) given the lack of data for the region. 
The optimal approach to assess pluvial hazard would have been to simulate 10,000 stochastic years, 
however, this solution would be impractical at this scale in terms of computation time and 
resources 
 
  Recommendations on users and applications 
The accuracy of any model result is affected by the input data quality and availability and the model 
assumptions. In our application, the pluvial flood hazard  has greater uncertainty than the fluvial 
flood hazard, because there are more uncertain localized factors that can influence pluvial flooding 
but are not represented in our model. The same is true for defended flood hazard, whose accuracy 
is limited by the quality and availability of hydraulic defense structures information.  2D hydraulic 
models are known to perform better on large rivers and , therefore, fluvial flood hazard maps are 
expected to be more accurate in large floodplains than in mountainous headwater areas . Because 
of these limitations,  caution should be used for the interpretation of the h azard estimates at the 
very local scale , also considering the spatial resolution of 90m that does not allow for a detailed 
assessment of flood footprints at the local scale . The use of these data is , therefore,  not 
recommended for detailed planning or operational decision as well as for engineering-level analysis 
of specific assets. That been said, we are fully convinced the hazard estimates computed herein are 
appropriate for assessing regional flood risk, which is the final objective of this study.
